title: The Complexity of Dynamical Correlators: Operator Shadows and Exponential Learning Separations
authors: Shao-Hen Chiew, Armando Angrisani, Zoe Holmes
abstract: Quantum platforms can realize many-body dynamics beyond classical simulation yet complete readout remains intractable: the cost of extracting accessible information scales exponentially with system size. Classical shadows and Bell sampling offer scalable, multi-observable estimation from randomized or entanglement-assisted measurements. Here we aim to push these ideas beyond static snapshots to dynamical correlators, including out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) and two-point functions. In particular, we introduce the notion of the shadow of an operator, defined as the classical shadow of the vectorized time-evolved operator. Pauli operator-shadows enable simultaneous estimation of all local OTOCs, while Clifford operator-shadows enable efficient simultaneous estimation of all two-point correlators. Alternatively, Bell sampling allows one to simultaneously compute all diagonal OTOCs. We also prove information-theoretic lower bounds for learning OTOCs, fully characterizing their query complexities in many cases, and yielding exponential separations that formalize when the vectorized approach provides measurement-efficiency advantages.
summary: The paper develops advanced measurement techniques using 'operator shadows' to efficiently estimate dynamical quantum correlators like OTOCs and two-point functions. By establishing both algorithmic upper bounds and rigorous information-theoretic lower bounds, the authors precisely characterize the minimum resources needed for these measurements. This advances our ability to diagnose complex many-body dynamics from limited experimental data.
main_problem: The core problem is developing scalable measurement protocols to estimate complex dynamical quantum correlators, such as OTOCs and two-point functions, which are intractable via full state readout.
main_result: The authors introduce the 'operator shadow' technique, achieving efficient estimation of large families of these correlators using Pauli or Clifford shadows. They also establish information-theoretic lower bounds proving the measurement efficiency advantages of their vectorized approach.
method: They utilize randomized measurements (shadow techniques) applied to time-evolved operators, recasting Heisenberg dynamics into state preparation tasks in the Schrödinger picture. The analysis involves deriving and matching upper bounds with rigorous information-theoretic lower bounds.
model_or_system: The work applies to general many-body quantum systems whose dynamics are governed by unitaries or quantum channels ($\mathcal{E}$). The focus is on estimating expectation values involving time evolution, such as $	ext{tr}(O(t) P O(t) Q)/2^n$.
key_observables: Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlators (OTOCs), two-point Pauli correlators ($	ext{tr}(P_k P_l(t))/2^n$), and general Process Tomography Matrix (PTM) elements.
important_parameters: The complexity bounds depend on the system size ($n$ qubits), the weight of operators ($w$), the number of observables to estimate ($M$), and the desired precision ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to prepare states corresponding to time-evolved operators via unitaries applied to maximally entangled states, and that lower bounds can be derived by distinguishing specific quantum states.
figures_summary: Figure 1 summarizes various protocols for learning OTOCs based on adaptivity, quantum memory requirements, and ancilla access, comparing different shadow techniques.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need to measure dynamics beyond static snapshots. It introduces the operator shadow framework, details specific algorithms (Pauli/Clifford shadows) for OTOCs and two-point functions, and culminates in deriving rigorous information-theoretic lower bounds that characterize the optimal query complexity.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical toolkit for quantum characterization, directly addressing how to extract complex dynamic information from limited experimental measurements—a critical bottleneck in simulating real physical systems like quantum processors or condensed matter models.
